newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey raises stakes in Cyprus missile crisis.
newsitem.headline: Turkey raises stakes in Cyprus missile crisis.

text.p: Turkey has raised the threat of the first major military conflict on Cyprus since its 1974 invasion in a row over plans by the Cypriot government to deploy anti-aircraft missiles.
Two days of verbal bombardment by Turkish officials culminated in a threat on Thursday to knock out the Russian-made missile system in a military strike.

"Ankara is seriously considering an operation against the missile launchers when the time comes if Turkey's warnings to the Greek Cypriot administration are not heeded," the state-run Anatolian news agency said.
The Cypriot government and Greece, which is committed to its defence, shrugged off the threat.
But Turkish commentators said Ankara's views should not be taken lightly.
"The situation really is serious. To be honest it's as serious as carrying the risk of war," analyst Sami Kohen wrote in the newspaper Milliyet on Thursday.
The Russian S-300 surface-to-air missiles could neutralise Turkish air superiority on the island.
Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup attempt backed by Athens, where a military government wa sin power.
There are 30,000 Turkish troops in the northern third of Cyprus while the internationally recognised Cyprus government controls the Greek Cypriot south.
Cyprus has declared its intention to buy the missiles to prevent possible Turkish air strikes but has not said how many will be deployed or when.
Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said Turkey would use all possible means to prevent the missiles being deployed.
Anatolian said Tayan drew a parallel with the Cuban missile crisis in 1962 when Russia tried to station missiles on Cuba.
Kohen said in Milliyet that Ankara had both diplomatic and military options under consideration.
"In the military field plans covering several possibilities are being prepared," Kohen said.
The United States warned Turkey against launching any attack on Cyprus.

"This is no time for the Turkish government to be making wild and dramatic statements which will not be supported by any sensible member of the international community," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington.
"It would be completely out of bounds for Turkey to take this action."
The United States, which has exerted pressure on Nicosia to cancel the missile deal, is to send an envoy to the island at the weekend to try to reduce the tension.
Western governments fear the missile row, coupled with recent killings in the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone dividing Cyprus, could reignite old conflicts between NATO members Greece and Turkey.

Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis said Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides would be invited to Athens for talks on the issue this month but added there was no cause for concern that a new crisis would erupt between Greece and Turkey.
"We would be playing Turkey's game if we showed particular worry over this and were swept into an atmosphere of crisis," Simitis told reporters.
